label: Lefschetz Pencils and Morse Theory
notes: Welcome to our lecture on Lefschetz pencils, a fundamental tool in the topology of algebraic varieties. Our goal today is to study how any projective variety can be systematically fiber-wise decomposed over a projective line, turning its global topological structure into a dynamic family of hypersurfaces. We will discuss how to resolve the base locus of a pencil using blow-ups, classify the singular fibers using the holomorphic Morse lemma, and study the monodromy action on cohomology through the Picard-Lefschetz formula. This theory, pioneered by Solomon Lefschetz, lies at the heart of modern complex algebraic geometry and Hodge theory.

label: The Lefschetz Pencil Arc
notes: This slide outlines our roadmap through Chapter 2. We begin by defining linear systems and pencils of hyperplanes. Then we prove that generic pencils have very nice properties, specifically isolated quadratic singularities. We will show how blowing up the base locus resolves the map into a true morphism, study the local topology near the singularities using the holomorphic Morse lemma, and introduce the vanishing cycles. This allows us to define the monodromy action, prove the Picard-Lefschetz formula, and finally study the decomposition of cohomology into primitive and vanishing parts.

label: Linear Systems and Lefschetz Pencils
notes: Lefschetz's key insight was that we can study the topology of a variety X by cutting it with a family of hyperplanes. A generic pencil of hyperplanes intersects X in a family of hypersurfaces that are smooth for almost all parameters, except for a finite number of critical values where a single ordinary double point appears. The existence theorem guarantees that such pencils always exist. Near these isolated singularities, the variety looks like a complex quadratic cone, which can be analyzed using local coordinates from the holomorphic Morse lemma.

label: Resolving the Rational Map via Blowup
notes: A pencil of hyperplanes in projective space all intersect along a codimension-two subspace called the axis of the pencil. Consequently, the rational map from X to the projective line is not defined on the base locus B, which is the intersection of X with the axis. To resolve this rational map, we blow up X along B. The blown-up variety, which we denote as X-tilde, maps holomorphically to the projective line. The hyperplanes, which were intersecting along the axis, now become disjoint fibers in the blowup, and the exceptional divisor E maps as a smooth projective bundle over the base locus, providing a natural section.

label: Holomorphic Morse Lemma & Singular Fibers
notes: The holomorphic Morse lemma gives us a powerful local model for the degenerations. Near an isolated critical point, the family of hypersurfaces can be written in a simple quadratic form. This is the direct complex analogue of the classical Morse lemma in real differential topology. By restricting our variables to the real subspace, we see a sphere of dimension n-minus-one whose radius is the square root of t. As t approaches zero, the radius shrinks, and the sphere collapses to a point at the critical value, which is why we call it the vanishing sphere.

label: Vanishing Spheres and Monodromy Action
notes: When we wind around a critical value in the base space, the fibers undergo a topological deformation. Although the fibers are homeomorphically identified after a full loop, the identification is not the identity on homology. Instead, it is given by the Picard-Lefschetz formula. If a cycle alpha does not intersect the vanishing cycle delta, it remains completely unchanged. If it does intersect, it is shifted by a multiple of the vanishing cycle. The coefficient depends on the topological intersection number of alpha and delta. This gives us a highly explicit matrix action for the monodromy.

label: Vanishing and Primitive Cohomology
notes: The Picard-Lefschetz formula allows us to decompose the middle cohomology of the smooth fiber into two orthogonal subspaces under the intersection pairing. The first is the primitive cohomology, which consists of classes that are invariant under the monodromy action. These classes actually come from global cohomology classes on the entire variety X. The second is the vanishing cohomology, which is the subspace spanned by the vanishing cycles. The global monodromy group acts irreducibly on the vanishing part, giving us a beautiful algebraic splitting that is compatible with the Hodge decomposition.

label: Worked Example: Monodromy and Hodge Ledger
notes: Let's perform a concrete numerical check using the data from our notebook. For a toy four-dimensional Kähler manifold, the Betti numbers are one, two, eleven, two, and one. The second Betti number is eleven, and the middle Hodge numbers are one, nine, and one. The monodromy around a loop acts on the middle cohomology, which has dimension eleven. Our invariants check verifies that this monodromy preserves the symplectic intersection pairing with zero residual error. Furthermore, the odd Betti numbers are even, satisfying the topological requirement for a Kähler manifold. This confirms the mathematical consistency of our model.

label: Pitfalls in Lefschetz Pencil Theory
notes: As you study Lefschetz pencils, there are a few common pitfalls to avoid. First, do not confuse the base locus of the pencil with its critical locus. The base locus is where all hyperplanes in the pencil intersect, and generically it is completely smooth. The critical points, on the other hand, are the isolated points where hyperplanes become tangent to the variety. Second, do not assume monodromy is trivial just because the total space X is simply connected. The base space of the fibration is a punctured projective line, which has a very rich fundamental group, leading to complex and non-trivial monodromy. Finally, remember that monodromy only preserves the primitive cohomology classes, while the vanishing classes are actively transformed.

label: Problem Set: Lefschetz Pencils
notes: We close with a tiered problem set designed to solidify your understanding. The first problem, suitable for undergraduates, asks you to explicitly compute the blowup of the projective plane at a single point, showing how it relates to the Hirzebruch surface F-one. The second problem is a graduate-level exercise where you will compute the monodromy for a pencil of quadric curves, analyzing the three singular fibers where a conic degenerates into a pair of lines. The third, research-level problem, asks you to prove the transitivity of the monodromy action on the set of vanishing cycles and deduce that the vanishing cohomology is an irreducible representation under this action.
